title: Borrowing & Lifetimes
summary: Lend values without giving them away. Learn shared and mutable references, why you can't alias and mutate at once, slices, and how lifetimes stop references from dangling.

quest.title: Lending the Ledger
quest.story:
You won the ledger. Now every officer on the Crab Fleet wants to look at it: the navigator to read the route, the cook to count the rum, the captain to scribble new plunder into it.

Handing the ledger over for good is out of the question. You learned that the hard way. Instead you **lend** it. The ship's articles about lending are strict:

- Any number of officers may **read** the ledger at the same time.
- Only **one** officer may **write** in it, and while they write, nobody else may even look.
- Whoever borrows the ledger must give it back before it leaves port. A note that says "the ledger is in the captain's cabin" is worthless once the cabin is gone.

*Rustc* the parrot enforces these articles at compile time, and it squawks in a new dialect now: E0502, E0499, E0106, E0515.

Learn to lend the ledger without losing it, and the quartermaster's quill is yours.

concepts.title: Shared references: &T
Mutable references: &mut T
Aliasing XOR mutation
concepts.body:
The core rule: at any moment a value has **either** any number of `&` borrows **or** exactly one `&mut` borrow, never both.

```rust
let mut ledger = vec![1, 2];
let first = &ledger[0];
ledger.push(3);       // error[E0502]: cannot borrow as mutable
println!("{first}");  // because it is also borrowed as immutable
```

Why so strict? `push` may reallocate the buffer, and then `first` would point at freed memory. Two `&mut` at once are rejected too (**E0499**), because two writers could invalidate each other's view.

The usual fixes: finish reading before you write, copy out the small value you need (`let first = ledger[0];` for an `i32`), or compute first and mutate afterwards.

concepts.title: Borrows end at their last use
Slices: &str and &[T]
concepts.body:
A **slice** is a borrowed view of part of a sequence: a pointer plus a length.

- `&str` views text. String literals are `&str`, and `&String` coerces to it.
- `&[T]` views elements. `&Vec<T>` and arrays coerce to it.
- `&mut [T]` lets you change the elements in place, but not add or remove them.

```rust
let line = String::from("gold: 30");
let name: &str = &line[..4];        // "gold"
let shares = vec![5, 10, 20];
let tail: &[i32] = &shares[1..];    // [10, 20]
```

Prefer `&str` and `&[T]` parameters over `&String` and `&Vec<T>`. They accept more callers and say exactly what you need.

concepts.title: Lifetimes: references can't outlive their owner

visual.title: Lending the ledger

steps.note: ledger owns a heap buffer holding two numbers.
peek borrows ledger. While a shared borrow is alive, ledger is frozen: nobody may change it.
Reading through peek is fine. This is peek's last use, so the shared borrow ends right here.
peek is no longer used, so a &mut borrow is allowed. pen has exclusive access: ledger can't even be read directly now.
push needs more room, so the Vec moves its elements to a bigger buffer and frees the old one. A live peek would now point at freed memory. That's why E0502 exists.
pen's last use was the push, so the &mut borrow has ended. ledger is no longer frozen and can be read again: it prints 3.
End of main: ledger is dropped and frees its buffer. The references owned nothing, so they free nothing.

challenges.title: Reading while writing
challenges.story: The navigator holds a finger on the first line of the ledger while the captain adds a new one.
challenges.prompt: Read the program. What happens when you compile and run it?

choices.label: Compile error E0502: cannot borrow `ledger` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
Compile error E0499: cannot borrow `ledger` as mutable more than once at a time
Compile error E0382: `ledger[0]` was moved into `first`
It compiles, but panics at runtime because `first` points at freed memory

hints: `first` is a reference into the vector. When is it used for the last time?
`push` takes `&mut self`. Is there another borrow of `ledger` alive at that moment, and of which kind?
A shared borrow (`first`) is still alive when `push` asks for a mutable one. Rust rejects that at compile time, so it never gets the chance to dangle at runtime.

challenges.title: Peek, then grab
challenges.story: The cook peeks at the rum count, then the bosun grabs the ledger to add five barrels.

choices.label: Compile error E0502: `rum` is borrowed by `peek` until the end of `main`
Compile error E0499: `rum` is borrowed mutably twice

hints: How long does the borrow in `peek` last: to the end of the block, or to its last use?
`peek` is never used after the first `println!`. Is anything still borrowing `rum` when `grab` is created?
Borrows end at their last use, so `&mut rum` is allowed. `*grab += 5` changes `rum` itself, not a copy.

challenges.title: Too many quills
challenges.story: Two officers grabbed the ledger at once, and a third is still pointing at a line. *Rustc* refuses to let the ship sail.
challenges.prompt:
This program does not compile. Make it compile and print exactly:

```text
first: gold
["gold", "rum (checked)", "maps", "silk"]
```

Rules:
- Keep the borrows `last` and `first` and use them as they are used now. Fix it by **reordering** statements so the borrows don't overlap.
- No `.clone()`, `.to_string()` or `.to_owned()`.
hints: There are two errors. Read each one: which borrow is still alive when `ledger` is borrowed again?
`last` is a `&mut` borrow that lives until `last.push_str(...)`. `first` is a `&` borrow that lives until it is printed. Neither may overlap a `push`.
Move `last.push_str(" (checked)");` above the first `push`, and move `println!("first: {first}");` above the second `push`.

No .to_string(): copying the text dodges the borrow instead of fixing it.
No .to_owned(): copying the text dodges the borrow instead of fixing it.
Don't copy entries out of the ledger: reorder the borrows instead.

challenges.title: Notes that point nowhere
challenges.story: The old quartermaster wrote two helper functions. One forgot to say where its answer comes from. The other hands out a note to a cabin that sinks the moment the function returns.
challenges.prompt:
Neither function compiles. Fix both:

- `longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str` returns whichever input has more bytes, and `a` on a tie. It must keep returning a **borrowed** `&str` that points into one of its inputs. Add the lifetime annotation it needs.
- `title(name: &str)` returns `"Captain "` followed by the name. It builds a new string, so it can't return a reference to it. Change the return type so it hands the new string over.

Hidden tests call both functions directly. One of them keeps the result of `longest` after the call, as a `&str`.
hints: Read the error codes. E0106 is about `longest`, and E0515 (which shows up once E0106 is gone) is about `title`.

`longest` returns one of its inputs, but rustc can't tell which. Name one lifetime and use it on both inputs and on the result. `title` creates `t` inside the function, and `t` is dropped when the function returns.
`fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str`, and `fn title(name: &str) -> String { format!("Captain {name}") }`.

challenges.title: Slicing the manifest
challenges.story: The purser needs three small tools that look at parts of the manifest without copying any of it.
challenges.prompt:
Implement the three functions. None of them allocates. They return views into their input or change it in place:

- `first_word(line: &str) -> &str`: the text before the first space, or the whole line if there is no space. `"gold 30"` gives `"gold"`, `""` gives `""`.
- `last_n(entries: &[u32], n: usize) -> &[u32]`: the last `n` elements, or all of them if there are fewer than `n`.
- `add_bonus(shares: &mut [u32], bonus: u32)`: add `bonus` to every element, in place.

Hidden tests call all three directly and check that the returned slices point into the input.
hints: Slicing syntax: `&s[..i]` is everything before index `i`, and `&v[start..]` is everything from `start` to the end.

`str::find(' ')` returns `Option<usize>`. For `last_n`, compute the start index carefully: `len - n` underflows when `n > len`, but `len.saturating_sub(n)` doesn't. To change elements, loop with `for s in shares.iter_mut()` and write `*s += bonus`.
`match line.find(' ') { Some(i) => &line[..i], None => line }`, `&entries[entries.len().saturating_sub(n)..]`, and `for s in shares.iter_mut() { *s += bonus; }`.

forbid.message: No .clone(): lend the value with & or &mut instead of copying it.
No .to_vec(): return a view into the input, not a copy.

challenges.title: Find the entry
challenges.story: The captain shouts a prefix across the deck, "rum!", and wants a finger on the matching ledger line. The shout fades at once, but the finger must stay on the ledger.
challenges.prompt:
Write `find_entry`. It takes a ledger `&[String]` and a prefix `&str`, and returns `Option<&str>`: the **first** entry that starts with the prefix, borrowed from the ledger, or `None`.

```rust
let ledger = vec![String::from("gold: 30"), String::from("rum: 12")];
assert_eq!(find_entry(&ledger, "rum"), Some("rum: 12"));
```

The returned `&str` borrows from the **ledger only**. The hidden tests drop the prefix before they use the result, so you have to write the lifetime annotations that say so. An empty prefix matches the first entry.

Keep a `fn main()`; it can call `find_entry` or stay empty. After the tests pass, the tutor judges whether your solution is idiomatic.
challenges.starter:
// Write find_entry here: (ledger: &[String], prefix: &str) -> Option<&str>

fn main() {}
hints: Two references go in and one comes out, so lifetime elision can't decide for you. Which input can the result actually point into?
Put a lifetime `'a` on `ledger` and on the result, and leave `prefix` with its own, unnamed lifetime. `str::starts_with` does the matching.
`fn find_entry<'a>(ledger: &'a [String], prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a str>`, with a body like `ledger.iter().find(|e| e.starts_with(prefix)).map(|e| e.as_str())`.

forbid.message: No .clone(): lend the value with & or &mut instead of copying it.
No .to_string(): copying the text dodges the borrow instead of fixing it.
No .to_owned(): copying the text dodges the borrow instead of fixing it.

challenges.rubric: Idiomatic borrowing: the signature is fn find_entry<'a>(ledger: &'a [String], prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a str>. The lifetime ties the result to the ledger only; the prefix keeps its own elided lifetime. Taking &Vec<String> or &String instead of &[String] / &str costs points. Returning an owned String or cloning entries is not acceptable. The body uses str::starts_with and either an iterator chain (iter().find(..).map(String::as_str) or similar) or a plain for loop with an early return Some(entry); both are fine. Deduct points for index-based loops (for i in 0..ledger.len()), manual byte comparisons instead of starts_with, unnecessary 'static or extra lifetime parameters, or .unwrap() calls. Readability matters more than cleverness.

challenges.title: Boss: Lend the Ledger, Keep the Ledger
challenges.story: Plunder day. Every officer reads, writes, and points into the ledger at once, and the tally program falls apart under the strain. Make it sound and the quartermaster's quill is yours.
challenges.prompt:
The program reads plunder lines `name: amount` from stdin and prints a tally. It does not compile: it has **borrowing and lifetime bugs**. Fix it so that, for the input

```text
gold: 30
rum: 12
gold: 5
maps: 1
bad line
```

it prints exactly:

```text
entries: 4
gold x35
rum x12
maps x1
fleet x48
richest: gold
```

Rules:
- Lines that don't parse as `name: amount` are skipped. Names and amounts are trimmed.
- Totals keep the order in which names first appear. The last total is `fleet`, the sum of all the others.
- `richest` is the name with the biggest total, not counting `fleet`. Ties keep the first. With no entries it prints `richest: none`.
- Keep the five functions. You may change their signatures and bodies.
- Totals keep borrowing names from the input text: no `.clone()`, `.to_string()`, `.to_owned()` or `String::from`.

Hidden cases include an empty input, a tie, and padded lines.
hints: Rustc reports these errors in waves: lifetime errors in signatures come first, borrow errors in bodies only after those are fixed. Fix one function at a time and recompile.

`label` builds a new string, so it must return an owned `String`. `richest` takes a slice of tuples that hold `&str`, so two lifetimes go in and elision gives up. Name the one the result really comes from: the names, not the slice.

`credit` stores `name` inside `totals`, so `name` must live as long as the names already in there: `fn credit<'a>(totals: &mut Vec<(&'a str, u32)>, name: &'a str, amount: u32)`. In `main`, you can't credit `totals` while you are iterating over it. Compute the fleet sum first, then credit it once.

`fn richest<'a>(totals: &[(&'a str, u32)]) -> Option<&'a str>` makes `top` borrow the input text, not `totals`, so you may still change `totals` afterwards. If you wrote `&'a [(&'a str, u32)]`, `top` keeps `totals` frozen and crediting `fleet` fails with E0502. Then: `let fleet: u32 = totals.iter().map(|t| t.1).sum(); credit(&mut totals, "fleet", fleet);`.

No .to_string(): copying the text dodges the borrow instead of fixing it.
No .to_owned(): copying the text dodges the borrow instead of fixing it.
No String::from: the totals should borrow names from the input text.

cards.front: What is the borrowing rule for a value at any one moment?
cards.back: **Either** any number of shared borrows (`&T`) **or** exactly one mutable borrow (`&mut T`), never both. Aliasing XOR mutation.

cards.front: What does E0502 mean, and why does `let f = &v[0]; v.push(x); use(f);` trigger it?
cards.back: E0502: cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable. `push` needs `&mut v` while `f` still borrows `v`. `push` may reallocate the buffer, which would leave `f` dangling.

cards.front: How long does a borrow last?
cards.back: Until the reference's **last use**, not until the end of the block (non-lexical lifetimes). Reordering code so all reads finish before a write often fixes E0502 and E0499.
Cannot borrow as mutable more than once at a time: a second `&mut` was created while the first is still used later. Finish using the first `&mut` before taking another.

cards.front: A function builds a `String` and tries to return `&s`. What does rustc say, and what is the fix?
cards.back: E0515: cannot return a reference to a local variable. The local is dropped when the function returns. Return the owned value instead: `-> String`.

cards.front: What does `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` promise?
cards.back: The returned reference is valid only while **both** inputs are. Without the annotation it's E0106 (missing lifetime specifier), because with two reference inputs rustc can't tell which one the result borrows from.

cards.front: Why prefer `&str` and `&[T]` parameters over `&String` and `&Vec<T>`?
cards.back: They accept more callers: literals, sub-slices like `&v[1..]`, arrays, and `&String`/`&Vec<T>` through coercion. They also say exactly what's needed: a read-only view.

cards.front: `fn find<'a>(xs: &'a [String], key: &str) -> Option<&'a str>`: why does `key` have no `'a`?
cards.back: The result only ever points into `xs`. Tying it to `key` too would keep `key` borrowed as long as the result is used, and callers couldn't drop a temporary key early. Put the lifetime only on the inputs the result can come from.
